title: What Mexico Can (and Cannot) Control
gist: Vanessa Rubio-Márquez argues Mexico has responded to Trump's ad-hoc, country-by-country bargaining with exceptional cooperation and retains one of the most favorable U.S. trade positions, but weakening institutions, falling investment, weak growth and a deteriorating fiscal and ratings profile are self-inflicted risks Mexico must fix.

insights.claim: Mexico sends more than 80% of exports to the United States, with nearly $900 billion of bilateral commerce a year and over $60 billion in annual remittances equal to 3.4% of GDP.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Mexico's extreme concentration makes US policy shifts the dominant macro risk for Mexican assets.
insights.locator: arguably no country has been as exposed

insights.claim: The author argues Trump-era U.S. policy has shifted from predictable rules to ad-hoc country-by-country bargaining on terms well beyond trade, and elements of this worldview may outlast Trump's term ending 2029.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Plan for persistent negotiation risk, not a one-off tariff episode.
insights.quote: the recent shift from a system of predictable rules to one of ad-hoc bargaining conducted country by country

insights.claim: Migrant encounters at the U.S.-Mexico border fell from over 2 million in 2022 to 237,538 in 2025, the fewest in 55 years, and U.S. fentanyl deaths roughly halved to about 37,400.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Mexico's delivery on border and drug metrics is its main bargaining chip.

insights.claim: Mexico sent 178 high-value criminals to the U.S., including Rafael Caro Quintero, and the army killed Jalisco New Generation Cartel head Nemesio Oseguera 'El Mencho' in February on shared U.S. intelligence.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Security concessions show willingness to preserve the partnership at almost any cost.

insights.claim: From January 2026 Mexico imposed tariffs of 5-50% on goods from countries without a free trade agreement, including China, India, South Korea and Vietnam, to address U.S. concerns about Chinese presence in North American supply chains.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Mexico is aligning its tariff regime with Washington, raising costs for Asian-sourced inputs.

insights.claim: Mexico negotiates on three tracks: a 54-point non-tariff barrier list from Marco Rubio, formal USMCA-related talks with four bilateral rounds since late May 2026 centered on trade deficit and rules of origin, and quiet back-channel offers to buy more U.S. goods and invest more across the border.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Autos rules-of-origin and 50% steel and aluminum tariffs are live headline risks.
insights.locator: On trade itself, Mexico has negotiated

insights.claim: The author sees possible permanent negotiation in which trade and non-trade issues such as security and water are constantly bargained.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Expect recurring headline risk rather than a final settlement.

insights.claim: About 87% of Mexican exports enter duty-free and the effective U.S. tariff averages about 3.4%, versus 21.7% for China, 10.9% for Brazil and 9.1% for India.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Mexico retains a relative tariff advantage, supporting nearshoring exporters.

insights.claim: Computer equipment, largely server and data-center hardware, has passed vehicles as Mexico's largest export to the U.S., and Mexico supplies about a quarter of U.S. imports of AI-related goods, matching Taiwan and far above China.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Mexico is a growing AI-hardware supply-chain node.

insights.claim: Mexico's red lines are keeping the trade framework intact, avoiding USMCA cancellation and wider tariffs, and preventing U.S. military action on its soil or U.S. interventions in domestic politics such as visa cancellations and extraditions of Morena figures.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Crossing these lines would remove Sheinbaum's room to manage tensions and trigger a harder line.

insights.claim: Since the Middle East conflict escalated in late February, the Strait of Hormuz blockade disrupted a fifth of world oil supply, raising oil, fertilizer and freight prices.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Energy and freight shocks feed through to import costs.

insights.claim: Higher oil prices are no longer a windfall for Mexico because crude exports fell from 1.1 million barrels per day in 2019 to about 0.3 million in 2026 while it still relies heavily on imported fuels, raising Pemex revenue but also import costs and pressuring public finances.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Oil spikes are net neutral-to-negative for Mexican fiscal and external balances.

insights.claim: A 2024 reform eliminated seven autonomous bodies including the competition regulator COFECE and energy regulator CRE, and judicial reform made Mexico the only country to elect its entire federal judiciary, with about 13% turnout among more than 99 million eligible voters.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Weaker checks raise regulatory and contract-enforcement risk for investors.

insights.claim: Mexico drew a record $40.8 billion of FDI in 2025 but only 18% was new investment, and federal physical investment fell 7.9% in real terms in the first half of 2026.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Headline FDI overstates fresh capital, mostly reinvested earnings.

insights.claim: Federal 2025 physical investment reached $40.1 billion versus a $44.7 billion budget, while Plan México implies about $46.2 billion annual needs through 2030 and gross fixed capital formation fell from 23.8% of GDP in 2024 to 22.4% in 2025.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Plan México's 28% of GDP investment target by 2030 looks hard to reach.
insights.locator: The point of departure is sensible

insights.claim: Plan México is a $277 billion project portfolio aiming to lift investment above 25% of GDP in 2026 and 28% by 2030, with 15 development poles targeting 300,000 jobs and a 30-day approval investment office.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Delivery versus announcement is the key monitorable.
insights.locator: The response has been Plan México

themes.theme: Growth, fiscal and ratings credibility gap

insights.claim: Mexico's GDP grew only 0.5% in 2025, contracted 0.3% quarter-on-quarter in Q1 2026 and rebounded 1.4% in Q2, prompting Banxico to lift its 2026 growth forecast from 1.1% to 1.6% and forecast 2.0% for 2027 with downside risks.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Growth is weak and reliant on a rebound base effect.

insights.claim: Interest payments rose from about 12% of government revenue in 2015 to more than 20% in 2025, the steepest increase in the Americas, with public debt rising from 43.6% of GDP in 2018 to 53.2% in 2025 and forecast at 54% in 2026.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Debt service squeezes fiscal space and supports ratings pressure.

insights.claim: Mexico has lost six combined notches across Moody's, Fitch and S&P since 2018, with Moody's and Fitch at the lowest investment-grade level and S&P one notch above; Moody's downgraded again in May 2026 and S&P moved its outlook to negative.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: A further downgrade risks losing investment grade and could hit Mexican issuers in 12-24 months.

insights.claim: Pemex received about $35 billion (1.9% of GDP) in federal support in 2025, and its supplier debt was $21.4 billion in the first half of 2026, nearly three times its 2018 level.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Pemex is a central source of sovereign credit pressure.
insights.locator: Although Pemex’s debt to suppliers fell

insights.claim: The author calls for regulatory certainty in energy, especially for data centers and semiconductor manufacturing, with predictable tariffs, clean-energy rules and transparent procurement.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Energy rule clarity is a gate for nearshoring and AI-infrastructure investment.

insights.claim: A property tax reform could raise roughly 2.8% of GDP of additional revenue without broad federal tax increases, versus property tax revenue of just $3.6 billion (about 0.2% of GDP) in 2024.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: A tax avenue that avoids a politically difficult broad reform before 2027 legislative elections.
insights.locator: In the absence of deeper solutions for Pemex

insights.claim: Double-digit minimum-wage increases are called unsustainable; the general minimum wage rose 256.5% between 2018 and 2026 and future raises should track inflation and productivity.
insights.speaker: VANESSA RUBIO-MÁRQUEZ
insights.so_what: Wage policy could constrain formal employment if not moderated.
insights.locator: Just as important, the government should call time
